topics.title: Prototypes and the Prototype Chain
topics.summary: Objects inherit properties from other objects through their prototype link.
topics.description:
Every JavaScript object has a hidden link, `[[Prototype]]`, to another object (or `null`). When you read a property the engine looks at the object itself first, then follows the link up the **prototype chain** until it finds the property or reaches `null`.

```js
const animal = { eats: true, walk() { return "walking"; } };
const dog = Object.create(animal);   // dog's prototype is animal
dog.barks = true;
dog.eats;      // true - found on the prototype
dog.walk();    // "walking"
```

### Important pieces
- `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` (or the legacy `obj.__proto__`) reads the prototype.
- `Fn.prototype` is the object that becomes the `[[Prototype]]` of instances created with `new Fn()`.
- `Object.prototype` sits at the top of nearly every chain; its prototype is `null`.
- Arrays inherit from `Array.prototype`, which inherits from `Object.prototype`. That is why `[].map` and `[].hasOwnProperty` both work.

### Own vs inherited
- Writing `dog.eats = false` creates an **own** property that shadows the inherited one.
- `Object.hasOwn(dog, "eats")` tests own properties.
- `for...in` also lists inherited enumerable properties.

### Why prototypes
Methods live **once** on the prototype and are shared by all instances, saving memory compared with copying them to every object.

### Classes are sugar
ES2015 `class` syntax is a cleaner way to write the same prototype mechanism; the engine still uses prototypes underneath.

### Dictionaries
`Object.create(null)` makes an object with **no** prototype - a pure key-value store without inherited keys like `toString`.
keyPoints: Every object links to a prototype; lookup walks the chain
Fn.prototype becomes the prototype of new instances
Chain ends at Object.prototype then null
Methods on the prototype are shared by all instances
class is syntactic sugar over prototypes
pitfalls: Modifying built-in prototypes (Array.prototype) can break other code
Replacing Fn.prototype after creating instances does not affect them

examples.title: Walking the chain

interview.a: The series of linked objects the engine searches when a property is not found on an object, moving from the object to its prototype and so on until null.
__proto__ (use Object.getPrototypeOf) is the actual link of an object to its prototype. prototype is a property of constructor functions that becomes that link for instances created with new.
It creates an object with no prototype, so it has no inherited methods and works as a clean dictionary.

topics.title: Constructor Functions and the new Keyword
topics.summary: Before classes, constructor functions with new built objects and shared prototype methods.
keyPoints: Constructor function + new creates linked objects
new creates an object, links the prototype, runs the function, returns it
Put shared methods on the prototype

pitfalls: Forgetting new makes this the global object
Defining methods inside the constructor creates a copy per instance

examples.title: Constructor with prototype methods

interview.q: What does the new keyword do?
interview.a: It creates an empty object, sets its prototype to the constructor's prototype, runs the constructor with this bound to the object and returns that object.

interview.q: Why put methods on the prototype instead of inside the constructor?
interview.a: One shared function is used by all instances, saving memory, instead of creating a new function for each object.

interview.q: How can you tell whether a function was called with new?
interview.a: Check new.target inside the function; it is undefined for a normal call.

topics.title: Classes
topics.summary: class syntax gives a clear way to define constructors, methods, getters and setters.
topics.description:
**Classes** (ES2015) are a cleaner syntax over prototypes and constructor functions.

```js
class User {
  constructor(name, age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
  }
  greet() {                 // on User.prototype
    return `Hi, ${this.name}`;
  }
  get isAdult() { return this.age >= 18; }       // getter
  set nickname(v) { this._nick = v.trim(); }     // setter
  static create(name) { return new User(name, 18); }  // static
}
const u = new User("Asha", 25);
```

### Key facts
- `constructor` runs on `new`; a class can have only one.
- Methods are placed on the prototype and are **non-enumerable**.
- Class declarations are **not hoisted** like functions (TDZ).
- Class bodies run in **strict mode**.
- Calling a class without `new` throws a `TypeError`.
- `typeof User` is `"function"`.

### Class fields (ES2022)
```js
class Counter {
  count = 0;                // public field
  inc = () => { this.count++; };   // arrow keeps this
}
```

### Class expressions
`const A = class { }` or a named class expression.

### instanceof
`u instanceof User` is `true`.

### Method `this`
Methods lose `this` when detached (`const f = u.greet`). Bind in the constructor or use arrow class fields (useful in React class components).

### Static members
`static` methods and properties belong to the class, not the instances - utility methods and factories.
keyPoints: constructor initialises instances, methods live on the prototype
getters and setters define computed properties
static members belong to the class itself
Classes are not hoisted and always strict
Class fields declare instance properties
pitfalls: Calling a class without new throws an error
Arrow-function fields are created per instance, not shared

examples.title: A small class

interview.q: Are JavaScript classes real classes like in Java?
interview.a: No. They are syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance; a class is a special function and methods live on its prototype.

interview.q: Difference between a static method and an instance method?
interview.a: A static method is called on the class itself (Account.compare) and has no instance this; an instance method is called on an object created from the class.

interview.q: What happens if you call a class without new?
interview.a: A TypeError is thrown: Class constructor cannot be invoked without 'new'.

topics.title: Inheritance with extends and super
topics.summary: Child classes reuse and override parent behaviour with extends and super.
keyPoints: extends sets up the prototype chain
super() must be called before this in a derived constructor
super.method() reaches the parent method
Static members are inherited
Prefer composition for flexible designs
pitfalls: Using this before super() throws a ReferenceError
Deep inheritance hierarchies are hard to change
Overriding a method and forgetting to call super when needed

examples.title: Animal and Dog

interview.q: What does super do in a class?
interview.a: In a constructor super(...) calls the parent constructor; in methods super.method() calls the parent's version of the method.

interview.q: Why must super() be called before this?
interview.a: In a derived class the parent constructor creates the object; this is not available until super() has run, so accessing it earlier throws a ReferenceError.
A design principle favouring building objects by combining small, focused pieces (has-a) rather than deep class hierarchies (is-a), which is more flexible.

topics.title: Private Fields, Static Members, Getters and Setters

Underscore prefix is only a convention

examples.title: Encapsulated wallet

interview.q: How do you create a private property in a class?
interview.a: Prefix the name with # (for example #balance). It can only be read or written inside the class body.

interview.q: What is the difference between a static and a private member?
interview.a: static decides who owns the member (the class instead of instances); # decides who can access it (only code inside the class). They can be combined: static #count.

interview.q: What are getters and setters useful for?
interview.a: They expose computed or validated properties with property syntax while running code behind the scenes, and let you make read-only properties by defining only a getter.
